scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Watusi developed in the United States as a solo craze dance during the early 1960s.
Its name was drawn from a former name for the Tutsi people of Africa, likely inspired by film portrayals of Tutsi dancers in the 1950 movie King Solomon's Mines or its sequel Watusi.
The trend achieved broad commercial visibility following R&B and pop song releases starting around 1961.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: As a popular fad dance, the Watusi functioned primarily as recreational social dance entertainment for youth and teenagers during the early to mid-1960s.
Today it is a historical tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Nudie Cuties 370 (https://archive.org/details/nc-370)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The Watusi is danced solo with the performer standing almost stationary and knees slightly flexed.
The dancer may execute one or two small rhythmic steps forward and backward.
The arms are held nearly straight with flat, aligned palms, moving alternately up and down in a vertical trajectory.
Watch for Vertical Arm Pump.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (TZdvihA7Y1A)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Solo dancer staying largely in place or moving within a small personal space.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance was performed to 1960s R&B, rock and roll, pop, and Latin jazz recordings.
Key hit singles associated with the dance include 'The Watusi' by The Vibrations (1961), 'The Wah-Watusi' by The Orlons (1962), and Ray Barretto's Latin jazz hit 'El Watusi' (1963).
Listen for the vocals, percussion.
The pulse is 4/4.
Upbeat early 1960s pop and R&B driven by vocal harmonies, rhythmic handclaps, or Latin jazz charanga percussion patterns.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The dance was performed in casual party, dance hall, and beach environments.
In American surf and beach culture during the 1960s, dancers performed outdoors on sand, incorporating beach aesthetic context into their movement styling.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key musical figures linked to the dance's popularity include vocal group The Orlons, singer Chubby Checker, Latin jazz musician Ray Barretto, and Mexican vocalist Julissa.
In Mexico, a Spanish-language rock and roll version of 'The Wah-Watusi' titled 'Mi rebeldito' was popularized by Julissa in 1963.
The Watusi is an American 1960s solo craze dance.
